Review Finds High Bias Across Artificial Intelligence Models for Lung Cancer Biomarkers

Across eighty-two primary research investigations published between 2018 and 2026, an exhaustive systematic review evaluating deep-learning and machine-learning frameworks for non-small cell lung cancer biomarker classification has revealed that sixty-seven percent of models exhibit a high overall risk of bias. Despite widespread claims of superior algorithmic discrimination and near-flawless concordance with expert clinical pathologists, the synthesis published in Discover Artificial Intelligence demonstrates that these performance metrics rest upon a methodologically fragile foundation. Conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 standards by researchers Adil Karim, Amine Berquedich, Sofia Semlali, El Habib Benlahmar, Sanaa El Filali, and Ahmed Zellou, the review represents the first formal appraisal to apply the Prediction model Risk Of Bias Assessment Tool across the broad spectrum of non-small cell lung cancer biomarker prediction. Rather than finding clinically ready diagnostic instruments, the evaluation highlighted pervasive structural vulnerabilities within participants and analysis domains that prevent routine translation into patient care.

The research team formulated their inquiry using the Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes, and Context framework to answer two central questions regarding the current technological state of artificial intelligence in oncology. Specifically, the authors sought to characterize how deep learning and machine learning are deployed across diverse biomarker categories, imaging modalities, and network architectures, while concurrently establishing which methodological factors govern whether reported performance metrics can be deemed trustworthy. To ensure comprehensive coverage of the literature, investigators queried seven major electronic databases: IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Springer Link, PubMed, Sage Journals, ScienceDirect, and BioMed Central. The initial search captured peer-reviewed studies published from 1 January 2018 through 31 March 2024, reflecting the emergence of specialized deep-learning approaches distinct from classical radiomics. A subsequent systematic update search executed in June 2026 incorporated literature through 31 May 2026, adding fourteen eligible studies to complement five records identified via backward citation tracking, ultimately yielding eighty-two primary studies.

Dual independent reviewers screened all imported titles, abstracts, and full texts against predefined eligibility rules, resolving conflicts through structured consensus with clinical and methodological specialists. While the review protocol was not prospectively registered on the PROSPERO database, the authors fixed their research objectives, search strings, eligibility thresholds, screening procedures, and data extraction forms prior to the formal database querying. The eighty-two qualifying studies distributed across five distinct thematic applications: survival prediction and analysis, treatment response forecasting, biomarker identification and analysis, imaging analysis for diagnosis and staging, and radiogenomics combined with transcriptomics. Architectural evaluation indicated that convolutional neural networks formed the single most common algorithmic family, accounting for twenty-eight studies or thirty-four percent of the corpus, followed by hybrid and multimodal architectures in twenty studies or twenty-four percent of the corpus. The remaining investigations integrated recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory networks, attention mechanisms such as Simple Temporal Attention, and specialized tissue classifiers.

Detailed examination across the thematic categories exposed consistent methodological fragmentation that severely limits direct comparability. In survival prediction, seven primary studies achieved reported concordance indices and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve metrics spanning 0.72 to 0.97 across overall survival, progression-free survival, and durable clinical benefit. However, these metrics were derived almost exclusively from internal hold-out splits or cross-validation on single cohorts without parallel calibration statistics. Investigations predicting treatment response to immunotherapy and chemo-immunotherapy similarly conflated disparate endpoints, treating pathological complete response, progression-free intervals, objective response rates, and immunohistochemical concordance interchangeably. While automated tumour-proportion scoring frameworks achieved impressive intraclass correlation coefficients reaching 0.873 against SP263 assays and 0.737 against 22C3 assays, fewer than half the studies explicitly confirmed whether validation cohorts were independent of training data. Similarly, diagnostic imaging pipelines extracting features from whole-slide histopathology and computed tomography rarely applied scanner harmonisation, leaving performance gains tethered to local acquisition settings.

Programmed death-ligand 1 and epidermal growth factor receptor mutations emerged as the primary targets of the surveyed predictive literature. Across sixteen studies investigating programmed death-ligand 1, algorithms addressed automated scoring on whole-slide stained tissue sections or non-invasive status inference from computed tomography and positron emission tomography scans. Digital pathology models demonstrated strong agreement with human pathologists, reporting Spearman correlation coefficients, intraclass correlations, or Lin concordance coefficients between 0.74 and 0.96, while radiographic models achieved reported area under the curve values between 0.80 and 0.97. Meanwhile, fifteen studies focused on epidermal growth factor receptor mutation detection directly from imaging, yielding clustered discrimination estimates from 0.81 to 0.94. Unlike other targets, receptor mutation radiogenomics featured multiple independent external validation cohorts, with studies reporting external test values of 0.78, 0.86, and 0.88. Notably, these externally derived metrics consistently occupied the lower boundaries of reported performance ranges, providing clear empirical evidence that internal validation metrics systematically overstate model accuracy.

Beyond the dominant focus on programmed death-ligand 1 and epidermal growth factor receptor mutations, the systematic review documented marked scarcity and fragility among models addressing other clinically actionable oncological targets. Only three investigations evaluated tumour mutational burden, yielding unverified area under the curve figures between 0.71 and 0.81. Studies targeting anaplastic lymphoma kinase and ROS1 gene rearrangements produced widely erratic discrimination figures, ranging from 0.73 on small single-institution samples to 0.995, and 0.84 to 0.85 across large real-world cohorts. Individual evaluations of KRAS, TP53, STK11, and epigenetic methylation signatures lacked external confirmation, with one KRAS radiomic pipeline collapsing from an internal F1 score of 0.67 to 0.41 on external data. The emerging domain of radiogenomics and transcriptomics, represented by complex autoencoders and multimodal U-Net architectures, faces severe technological bottlenecks. Fusing thousands of high-dimensional radiomic imaging features with vast transcriptomic profiles creates acute mathematical risks of overfitting and spurious correlation, compounded by an acute shortage of publicly accessible, perfectly matched multi-omic clinical repositories.

The formal methodological appraisal conducted through the twenty signalling questions of the PROBAST instrument uncovered pervasive structural weaknesses across the published predictive literature.
